plimsoll trainer · 05 / mcp + agents

Agent products

"Code mode" replaces a menu of read-only tools with one run_code tool and a small SDK the code can call. It makes the agent's interface narrower, not its permissions wider. The way to check that is to follow one tool call down through every layer and ask, at each one, what it can and cannot change.

01

One tool call, four layers

The model writes the tool arguments. The gateway, which authenticated the session, adds everything that carries authority. plimsolld checks the envelope and brokers the run. The domain API sees a route and a token, never the model. Choose what the model sends and watch where it stops.

    02

    Four identities, and where they may collapse

    An agent session, the tenant the gateway resolved it to, the principal plimsolld authenticates, and the subject the domain API reads from the minted token. The last two are built from the token the gateway holds, so the gateway's choice of token decides whether tenants stay apart downstream.

      03

      What the agent gets back

      One response shape for every run, including the ones where the code failed, so the agent can read its own mistake and revise. A refusal is a different shape, and it never echoes the code.

      04

      Model trust decides the floor

      The provider's name is not a policy. Decide the minimum wall for each kind of code, put it on every request as minimum_isolation, and read the tier every result reports.

      floor: none · process is fine

      Code you basically trust. Your own team's formulas, a demo, the inner loop while building the product. The in-process engine is instant and free; its escape lands in the daemon, which you have decided you can live with.

      floor: kernel

      Model-authored code over your API. Treat it as hostile unless a policy says otherwise. Verified runsc paints this mark and brokers both snippet and project grants. A plain container is not a hostile boundary, whatever its image is called.

      floor: vm

      Hostile code, or not on your hardware. One disposable microVM per run. Grants need the egress guard, and the template must already carry every tool, because the VM has no way to fetch one.

      05

      Ergonomics in the preamble, authority in the profile

      A small SDK can dress the generic client up as inventory.items.get(id). It runs inside the sandbox with the hostile code, so it is a convenience and a backstop, never the thing that enforces anything.

      The preamble (runs in the guest)

      • Friendly method names and argument encoding.
      • Clear errors for a misspelt id, before a round trip.
      • A .d.ts beside it, so the model writes against types.
      • Generated from the same OpenAPI document as the route list, by plimsoll-specgen, so the three cannot drift.

      The profile (held by plimsolld)

      • The upstream origin. The guest never learns it.
      • The exact routes, byte for byte; * for a whole segment.
      • Who may select it: allowed_callers.
      • Scopes, and how the credential is minted: one static bearer, or a fresh JWT per run with the principal as its subject.

      The guest can skip the preamble. A crafted script calls host.get directly with any path it likes. That is fine: the broker checks the route against the profile exactly as it would have anyway, and refuses the same way. The grant example in the repository does precisely this and is refused, then succeeds under a separate grant that lists the route. Nothing in the guest is load-bearing.

      06

      Before the tool goes live

      One successful demo proves the happy path. The launch is decided by what happens under overload, bad code, a weak backend, two tenants, one forbidden route and one downstream outage: each must produce a different, safe answer.
